newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banker urges Bonn to shift all debt to euro.
newsitem.headline: German banker urges Bonn to shift all debt to euro.

text.p: Dresdner Bank board member Gerd Haeusler warned Germany's strength as a financial centre could be undermined if the Bonn government failed to agree soon to convert all existing debt to the euro at its launch in 1999.

Haeusler told Reuters in an interview on Friday that an adverse decision on this could have "a disadvantageous effect on Germany as a financial centre and on the interest rate burden borne by the federal government".

Bonn, in common with other European states, is committed to issuing new debt in euros once the single currency is created in 1999. But it has lagged behind Paris in its commitment to convert existing debt from the launch date.

Europe plans to create its single currency from January 1, 1999 grouping those countries which meet economic goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation, public deficits and public debt as laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.
Germany, together with almost all other European states, is facing considerable problems in meeting the deficit criteria.

Haeusler, a former Bundesbank board member, said Bonn had put itself in a difficult position by assuring private investors -- who are heavily exposed to bond markets -- that they would not be directly confronted with the euro until notes and coins are issued in 2002.
But he warned that any failure to convert debt at the right time which resulted from this aim could prove "very dangerous".
The delay meant that Bonn risked not having German bonds considered as the benchmark for the euro-denominated bond market, he said.
"The benchmark will be decided in one of two ways. Either France and Germany get together and harmonise their issues and that forms the benchmark, or there will be a competition," Haeusler said.
"If there is to be a competition then we will soon have lost it unless there is a decision to convert."

Addressing the issue of Germany's problems in cutting its deficits and debt to the required level for participation in EMU, Haeusler said Bonn could benefit from conducting a sophisticated asset and liability management, including derivatives.
"Public authorities could make more use of derivatives in some areas to hedge their interest rate risk," he said.

The Bundesbank, which leans toward caution on such issues, has tended to warn against excessive use of hedging instruments, mindful of the huge losses which can arise if hedging strategies are not applied judiciously.

Admitting that Paris currently had some advantages over Frankfurt as a financial centre -- such as its relative freedom from the burden of minimum reserves -- Haeusler said he nonetheless believed Frankfurt would remain a leading financial centre within the euro region.

Noting the pre-eminence of the German future and options exchange, the Deutsche Terminboerse, in equities contracts, Haeusler said this gave Frankfurt a good chance of becoming a key centre for equities trading -- even though the equity culture in Germany is still underdeveloped.
"I am optimistic," he said. "In the next 10 years equities will play a greater role."

Predicting a higher number of bourse listings and increased investment in equities in Germany, Haeusler said increased use of shares as a means to secure retirement income would help boost interest in the share market.
"I see a gradual increase, at least in indirect investment in shares in Germany -- whether through funds or additional pension funding -- and hopefully in other areas as well," he said.
